Carter Hayes then came and went almost immediately, Evan Blake completing the catch, and that second wicket was important because it removed the possibility that Redmoor could use the first dismissal as a reset. Tyler Dean briefly gave the innings its only top-order scoring pulse, reaching a boundary and dragging the board into the teens, while Jordan Frost tried to play the captain’s stabilizing role beside him, but even that short passage never became control. The stand looked like a beginning only because everything around it was so thin. Nolan Hart entered the attack and changed the match from pressure into ownership. He bowled Tyler Dean before the third-wicket stand had time to become meaningful, and from that point the innings began to feel as though every Redmoor batter was being asked to bat twice: once against the ball, and once against the weight of dots that had already collected behind him. Jordan Frost made only a small captain’s hand before Connor Vale returned the innings to the same pattern, Caleb Brooks taking the catch, and Blake Mercer’s long, cramped stay summed up the problem perfectly. He occupied deliveries, but he could not transfer that occupation into scoring pressure. Nolan Hart removed him too, Isaac Rowe holding the chance, and now Redmoor were deep enough into trouble that the scoreboard itself began to act like a fielder. Parker Reid was pinned by Dylan Reed, whose spell from one end was almost suffocatingly economical, the kind of bowling that does not need constant wickets to dominate because it removes the batter’s easiest escape routes. Gavin Cross was bowled by Nolan Hart before he could become a lower-order repair option. Finley Tate was drawn into a stumping by Luke Bennett, another moment where pressure became footwork, footwork became error, and error became a wicket. Ethan Ward then fell without scoring, giving Nolan his fifth wicket and leaving Redmoor with almost nothing except a thin lower-order attempt to stretch the innings. Hudson Cole deserves some mention because his 9 from 31 was, in that context, a genuine act of resistance. It was not fluent and it was not enough to change the match, but it was the one late innings that suggested a batter had decided to fight time as much as the bowling. Aiden Bell stayed with him, unbeaten on 2, and together they took Redmoor past forty, which is a very small achievement in ordinary language but still more than most of the innings had looked likely to produce once the ninth wicket fell. Logan North finally ended the innings with another stumping for Luke Bennett, and Redmoor were all out for 42 in 24.2 overs. The score was not the result of one wild collapse alone. It was a full-innings squeeze. Connor Vale made the first cuts, Nolan Hart owned the center with five wickets for 12 in a spell that combined patience, control, and perfectly timed dismissals, Dylan Reed strangled scoring from the other end, and Logan North finished the last remaining resistance without letting the innings drag into anything more respectable. The most revealing detail is that Redmoor’s highest individual score was still in single figures, and their extras almost matched the best batting hand. That is what complete pressure looks like on a scorecard: not simply wickets, but the absence of any meaningful partnership, any set batter, or any phase in which the fielding side has to retreat. Kingsfield’s chase of 43 was never going to require fireworks, and they treated it correctly by refusing to make a tiny target more complicated than it needed to be. Owen Carter was watchful at the top, perhaps too watchful at times, and Parker Reid deserves credit for bowling him after a patient 6 that had done more to consume balls than to finish the chase. Yet even that wicket did not give Redmoor any real way back, because Luke Bennett had already shown enough touch to keep the innings moving and Mason Hart came in with exactly the right calm for the situation. Luke’s unbeaten 17 from 12 was the sharpest batting of the short chase, three boundaries placed with the confidence of a player who knew the target did not need to be chased in panic. Mason’s 12 not out was quieter but just as useful in function, keeping the line straight, collecting the singles and soft runs, and making sure the chase did not wobble after Owen’s dismissal. Redmoor’s bowling had a few moments of effort. Parker Reid took the only wicket and kept the early chase from being completely free. Hudson Cole was steady enough for a couple of overs. Blake Mercer’s brief spell, though, leaked the kind of wides that make a small defense impossible, and once those free runs arrived, the finish came quickly. Kingsfield reached 43 for 1 in 7.2 overs, winning by nine wickets with most of the batting order still padded up and unused. The match was decided almost entirely by the first innings, but that does not make the result shallow. Kingsfield won because they created pressure in layers: Connor Vale struck early, Nolan Hart made the middle collapse irreversible, Dylan Reed denied Redmoor any scoring release, Luke Bennett converted pressure into stumpings, and the chase was handled with professional restraint rather than unnecessary drama. Redmoor had only two tiny footholds, Tyler Dean’s early boundary and Hudson Cole’s late resistance, and neither lasted long enough to become a phase. Nolan Hart was the correct player of the match because his spell was the point at which a struggling innings stopped looking recoverable. Connor Vale opened the wound, Dylan Reed kept it from closing, but Nolan Hart was the bowler who made the collapse permanent, and that is why Kingsfield’s nine-wicket win felt even more decisive than the margin alone can express.

At Riverside Academy Ground in Brookfield, Eastmoor won the toss, chose to bat, and almost immediately found themselves in one of those short-format youth innings where a scoreboard can move quickly without ever really belonging to the batting side, because there were wides, there were flashes of strokeplay, there were a few boundaries that briefly made the surface look less hostile than it really was, but there was never a partnership substantial enough to let Eastmoor breathe. Northbrook’s new-ball work was not immaculate in the first couple of overs. Blake Turner sprayed enough outside the channel to give Eastmoor a few early gifts, and Will Pierce’s later defence would show that Eastmoor had bowlers capable of creating discomfort too, but the first innings was shaped by the fact that every time a batter hinted at getting set, Northbrook found the next cut. Parker Lane was the first to try to put some movement into the innings, punching an early boundary and making six at a brisk enough tempo to suggest Eastmoor might at least play with a little initiative, but Aaron Cole took him out before the opening stand had any depth. Oliver Hale, the wicketkeeper, was trying to survive rather than score, and when Blake Turner bowled him for three, the innings had already lost the small opening rhythm that the wides had helped create. Quinn Hayes came and briefly looked sharp, a boundary in a five-run stay, but Aaron Cole again found the answer, Felix Ward taking the catch, and that was the first real sign that Eastmoor’s problem was not just wickets, it was continuity. No one was staying long enough to make the next batter’s job easier. Rowan Foster, the captain, tried to impose some order, and Samuel Blake gave him a moment of support with a busy seven from six balls, yet that passage too dissolved before it could become a platform. Aaron’s third wicket, Samuel caught by Gabriel Hayes, left Eastmoor four down with only scattered batting evidence behind them. Thomas Hale then produced one of the more useful small hands of the innings, making eight and finding the rope once, and alongside Rowan he helped push the score toward the point where the innings at least had a shape rather than just a sequence of dismissals. Dylan Brooks ended that by bowling Thomas, and from there the match began shifting from Aaron Cole’s early damage to Caleb Foster’s finishing control. Rowan Foster’s sixteen was the closest Eastmoor had to an innings with authority in the upper half, though even that was more a collection of useful moments than a real command performance. He struck two boundaries, absorbed a few overs, and briefly looked like the one player who could drag the total past embarrassment and into something awkward. Caleb Foster removed him at exactly the right time, Julian Cross holding the catch, and that dismissal mattered because it stripped Eastmoor of the only remaining batter who could still claim to be constructing something. Umar Bennett tried to hang in and made six before Caleb pinned him in front. Victor Cross reached five and was then bowled by the same bowler. Will Pierce, left to manage the tail, showed some sense in staying there and finishing unbeaten on thirteen, the only lower-order player who gave the score any real extension, while Xavier Doyle arrived, struck one boundary, and vanished almost instantly. Zach Ward’s late nine from twelve, including two boundaries, gave Eastmoor their most energetic final flicker and lifted the total from a poor one into a merely small one, but Caleb Foster closed that too, Gabriel Hayes taking the catch as Eastmoor were dismissed for ninety-seven in the nineteenth over. The most revealing detail in the innings was not just the total, but the scale of the partnerships. The best stand was only fourteen. Several promising starts ended before the next over could settle. The batting runs added up to a thin card, and the fifteen extras, especially the thirteen wides, carried far too much weight for Eastmoor’s comfort. Northbrook’s bowling plan worked because it had two clear cutting edges. Aaron Cole owned the upper order, taking three important wickets in the first half of the collapse and making Eastmoor restart again and again. Caleb Foster then turned a damaged innings into a finished one, five wickets for nineteen, one maiden, and no wides, which mattered in a match where so many other bowlers on both sides occasionally leaked pressure. He did not simply polish off a tail after the game had already drifted. He removed the captain, then Umar Bennett, then Victor Cross, then Xavier Doyle, then Zach Ward, and each wicket came before Eastmoor could turn a small stand into a usable one. Chasing ninety-eight, Northbrook still had to avoid the classic mistake of treating a small target as if it had already been scored. Eastmoor did get one early moment when Xavier Doyle dragged Harrison Rowe forward and Oliver Hale completed the stumping, leaving Northbrook one down before the chase had fully settled. For a few deliveries, there was just enough uncertainty for Eastmoor to imagine that the match might become awkward if two more wickets came quickly. Isaac Bennett made sure that did not happen. His unbeaten forty-eight was the cleanest batting performance of the match because it understood exactly what the target required. He did not chase the finish in a burst of careless shots, and he did not retreat so far into caution that Eastmoor could build pressure around him. He took the early singles, used the loose ball through the off side, waited when Xavier Doyle was asking a better question, and then leaned into the chase once Julian Cross arrived with the more assertive tempo. Julian’s twenty-six from twenty-two was the innings that removed Eastmoor’s last realistic pressure point. He found boundaries early enough to stop the field from crowding Isaac, drove with purpose, and kept the scoreboard moving at a pace that made ninety-eight feel smaller every over. Their second-wicket stand of seventy-two was not just the largest partnership of the match; it was the first and only stretch in which one side looked fully in control for more than a handful of overs. Eastmoor’s bowling did not help itself. Will Pierce had effort but not enough threat. Umar Bennett’s short spell was untidy and expensive, carrying wides and no-balls at precisely the wrong moment. Samuel Blake kept things more orderly without creating a breakthrough. Zach Ward eventually removed Julian Cross, Samuel taking the catch, but by then the chase had already reached the edge of completion. Logan Pierce came in with barely any pressure left, made five not out, and Isaac Bennett stayed through to the finish as Northbrook crossed the line in the sixteenth over with eight wickets intact. Eastmoor’s defence suffered from the same disease as their batting: too many fragments, not enough sustained control. They had the stumping, they had Zach Ward’s late wicket, they had a few overs where the batters had to wait, but they also gave away fifteen extras in a chase of ninety-eight, and that made an already difficult defence nearly impossible. Northbrook won because they controlled the two decisive passages of the match. First, Aaron Cole and Caleb Foster refused to let Eastmoor build even one proper batting partnership. Then Isaac Bennett and Julian Cross supplied the single chase partnership the game required. Everything else was secondary. Eastmoor had small bursts from Rowan Foster, Will Pierce and Zach Ward, but no innings large enough to shape the day. Northbrook had one early strike bowler, one finishing strike bowler, one calm chase anchor, and one captain who killed the contest with a brisk support hand. That is why the eight-wicket result felt comfortable rather than merely efficient, and why Caleb Foster was the correct player of the match. His spell was the point at which Eastmoor stopped looking like a side that might scrape to a defendable score and became a side waiting for the innings to end. Once he had done that work, Northbrook’s chase only needed composure, and Isaac Bennett supplied it without allowing the game a second plot.

At Greenfield Academy Ground in Midlands, Southmere won the toss, chose to bat, and then spent most of the afternoon discovering that possession of first use was worth very little once Eastford found their working length, because this was not a collapse made from one frantic over or one wild passage of panic, it was a slow tightening, a careful taking-away of options, the kind of innings where every batter appeared to arrive with the previous problem still sitting at the crease. Rowan Miles was the first to go, pinned by Harvey Wells after a short, uncomfortable stay, and Harvey’s opening spell set the emotional temperature of the innings more than the scorebook alone can show. He was not spraying around looking for magic. He was keeping the ball in areas where the batter had to make decisions, and on a surface that did not exactly fly onto the bat, that was enough to make even simple survival look like work. Elliot Mason stayed for a long time, though “stayed” is doing nearly all the work in that sentence, because his four from thirty-three was less an innings than a long refusal to leave, a vigil that slowed the card without really giving Southmere any control. Caleb Turner briefly looked like the one top-order batter prepared to play a shot with conviction, striking a boundary and trying to disturb the field, but Ethan Vale removed him before that little burst could become a phase, and when Finley Brooks later ended Mason’s occupation, Southmere had already spent more than ten overs without finding anything like rhythm. Felix Clarke came and went under Gavin Stone’s pressure, and that was the beginning of the spell that decided the first innings. Gavin did not bowl as if he needed to blast everyone out. He bowled as if he understood that Southmere had almost no scoring release left, and he simply kept returning the ball to those areas where patience starts to turn against the batter. Owen Brooks was bowled before he could settle. Riley Vance gave Parker Lane a few overs of companionship but was still forced into a mistake. Sawyer Grant then produced the one stretch that gave Southmere a faint claim to resistance, putting together the best partnership of the innings with Parker and finding two boundaries that at least made Eastford adjust the field for a while. Parker Lane’s own innings was the thread holding the whole thing together, and even though twenty-one not out sounds small in isolation, in context it was the only truly durable batting effort Southmere produced. He was not fluent. He was not dominant. He was simply there: defending, waiting, using the occasional gap, trying to turn a broken score into something irritating enough to bowl at. The trouble was that nobody stayed long enough with him. Sawyer fell to Gavin, Theo Reed flashed briefly before Julian Cross removed him, and Ethan Vale came back to close the last two wickets, Victor Shaw bowled and Wyatt Brooks trapped in front without scoring. Southmere were all out for eighty-one in the thirty-first over, and even that total owed plenty to Eastford’s own indiscipline, because seventeen extras, most of them wides, kept the innings from looking as bare as the batting really was. That detail matters. Eastford were not perfectly clean. They gave Southmere little scraps of air. But the important thing was that they kept taking wickets before those scraps could become structure. Harvey Wells created the initial squeeze with three maidens and almost nothing conceded. Ethan Vale collected three wickets and cleaned up important pieces at both ends of the innings. Finley Brooks broke the long but stalled occupation from Elliot Mason. Julian Cross chipped out Theo Reed when the lower order was trying to add nuisance value. And Gavin Stone, with four wickets in his full spell, owned the middle, the exact part of the innings where Parker Lane was trying to build something around himself. That is why the award made sense. Gavin did not just add numbers after the work had been done; he prevented Southmere’s only possible recovery from becoming more than a stubborn delay. Chasing eighty-two, Eastford should have had a simple job, but small targets in youth cricket always carry a strange little danger, because one early wicket makes everyone look at the scoreboard twice, and two early wickets can make a chase feel far more complicated than it has any right to be. Southmere did manage to create that brief discomfort. Theo Reed bowled beautifully with the new ball, finding the sort of discipline Southmere had lacked too often with the bat, and Adrian Cole never looked free before Parker Lane completed the catch to give Theo the breakthrough. Brandon Miles had not been exactly fluent either, and when Rowan Miles trapped him lbw soon after, Eastford were two down with the target still not completely erased. That was Southmere’s one doorway back into the match. They had a tiny score to defend, they had two wickets, and they had at least one bowler who looked capable of making the ball talk. What they did not have was enough collective discipline. Wides kept arriving, no-ball pressure crept in once, and every time Eastford might have been asked to earn a run properly, Southmere found a way to soften the equation. Connor Reed understood that better than anyone. He did not try to finish the chase in a rush. His unbeaten eighteen was a small innings, but it was exactly the kind of small innings that wins low chases: compact, patient, almost stubbornly free of unnecessary risk. Dominic Shaw then came in and changed the tone completely. He was the only batter in the chase who looked capable of making the target shrink in visible chunks, driving cleanly, using the short ball well enough, and striking the one six that finally made Southmere’s fielders feel as if the match was escaping rather than merely slipping. The third-wicket stand between Dominic and Connor did the real finishing work, not because it was huge in normal terms, but because in a chase of this size it gave Eastford certainty. Connor closed one end. Dominic advanced the other. The extras kept coming in the background like an unwanted echo of Southmere’s own batting innings. By the time Dominic was finally caught off Wyatt Brooks, the game had already been reduced to formalities. Ethan Vale arrived and ended it quickly, striking his first scoring shot with the clarity of a player who knew there was no value in dragging the afternoon out any longer, while Connor remained there to make sure nothing strange happened at the other end. Eastford reached eighty-two for three in the fifteenth over and won by seven wickets, a margin that felt fully accurate to the cricket despite the slightly uneasy opening to the chase. Southmere had fought in fragments: Parker Lane’s not-out resistance, Sawyer Grant’s brief support, Theo Reed’s excellent opening spell, Rowan Miles finding one lbw shout that stuck. But fragments were all they had. Their batting never found a partnership large enough to matter beyond delay, their extras gave Eastford too much of the chase for free, and their bowlers could not support Theo Reed long enough to make a tiny target feel genuinely alive. Eastford, by contrast, handled the day in phases. Harvey Wells pressed the top. Gavin Stone tore the middle out of the innings. Ethan Vale finished the tail. Connor Reed and Dominic Shaw then absorbed the only small scare in the chase and turned the result into process. So the match was not won by glamour, and it did not need to be. It was won by pressure, by timing, by enough control to make Southmere restart almost every few overs, and by the calm to avoid making eighty-two look like one hundred and twenty. Gavin Stone was the correct player of the match because his spell sat exactly where the match could still have changed shape. Parker Lane was trying to make Southmere awkward. Sawyer Grant briefly gave him help. Gavin removed that help, kept removing the next attempt after it, and made sure Eastford walked into the chase with a target that even a slightly nervous start could not spoil.

At Brookfield Oval in Fairhaven, Westmoor chose to field first and eventually won by four wickets, but the shape of the match was more layered than that margin suggests, because Ridgefield were not simply rolled over from the first over and Westmoor did not chase the target without turbulence; instead the game passed through three distinct moods, an early Ridgefield repair after a poor start, a long middle squeeze led by Lewis Archer, and then a chase that looked almost settled before Dylan Foster dragged a little late disorder back into it. The first innings began with exactly the sort of dismissal Westmoor wanted after choosing to bowl, Toby Lane hitting the right length early and removing Aiden Moss before Ridgefield had any real rhythm, but Blake Warren immediately changed the temperature of the innings. He was busy, almost too eager at times, but his twenty-four from twenty balls gave Ridgefield the only truly sharp top-order burst they managed all morning, four boundaries and a lifted shot that forced Westmoor to adjust the field sooner than they would have liked. Caleb Stone came in and looked far more durable, less frantic than Blake, much clearer about the long work required, and for a little while those two gave Ridgefield a way out of the opening dent. Toby returned to remove Blake, Kian Brooks taking the catch, and that wicket stopped the early scoring from becoming a full platform, but it did not yet give Westmoor control. That control had to be earned later, because Caleb Stone and Dylan Foster then produced Ridgefield’s one genuinely substantial passage of batting. Caleb was the player most likely to turn the innings into something competitive, not because he scored wildly, but because he kept finding the right moments to release pressure. His forty-nine from sixty-one had enough boundary threat to make the field move, and the two clean hits over the rope gave the stand an energy Dylan Foster could not have supplied on his own. Dylan’s role was different. He was slower, tighter, more about occupation than command, but that mattered in the context of Ridgefield’s innings. He stayed with Caleb through the only phase when the batting side looked as though it might build a total large enough to make the chase uncomfortable. Their stand reached sixty-one, and for a time Westmoor were having to bowl at two batters who had taken the innings beyond survival and into construction. The turning point came when Kian Brooks removed Caleb just short of his fifty, Mason Cole taking the catch, because that dismissal cut away the only Ridgefield batter who looked capable of pushing the score toward something meaningfully above the mid-hundreds. From there Lewis Archer began to control the match. He did not do it with noise. He did it with a spell that kept shrinking Ridgefield’s options. Dylan Foster, after all that patient work, was bowled before he could turn occupation into acceleration. Ethan Hart followed after a brief, careful stay, also beaten by Lewis, and that pair of wickets changed the innings from a possible platform into a repair job all over again. Finley Rhodes and Gavin Reed could not rebuild it. Harvey Stone removed Finley, then Lewis came back to take Gavin, and suddenly Ridgefield had slipped from a position that still carried promise into one where every lower-order run felt like salvage. Hayden Cole and Isaac Dale did give them one more stubborn partnership, not flashy, not fluent, but useful because it dragged the total away from complete underperformance. Hayden found a couple of boundaries in his thirteen, Isaac wore down a few overs for seven, and together they added enough to push Ridgefield near the kind of score that at least asks a chase to concentrate. Harvey broke that stand by trapping Hayden, Mason Cole then finished the last stretch by bowling Isaac and having Logan Vale caught, and Ridgefield were all out for one hundred and fifty-two in the forty-third over. It was a total made from one serious hand, one early spark, one adhesive support innings and a few late scraps. The extras helped, but not enough to disguise the larger truth: after Caleb Stone went, Ridgefield never again looked like they owned the innings. Westmoor’s bowling card carried that message clearly. Toby Lane was expensive but made the first two incisions. Kian Brooks’ wicket of Caleb was a major structural break. Harvey Stone was the quiet destroyer of lower-order hope. Mason Cole closed the innings neatly. Lewis Archer was the reason the whole middle phase bent toward Westmoor. His ten overs brought three wickets for twenty-two, two maidens, and a kind of control that meant Ridgefield had to earn even the small runs after the one real stand was broken. Chasing one hundred and fifty-three, Westmoor then started as though they had no interest in letting a middling target acquire drama. Oliver Hayes and Callum Price put on seventy-six for the first wicket, and that partnership was the match’s second decisive passage. Oliver played the measured hand, not rushing, taking time to settle, then working the chase down through singles and the occasional boundary. Callum was brighter and more direct, cutting and driving whenever Ridgefield missed, and because he scored at the better tempo, Westmoor never got stuck even when Oliver absorbed a few quiet balls. Ridgefield also made the chase easier than it needed to be. Wides appeared at exactly the wrong time, and in a defence of this size those loose runs become more than mistakes; they become pressure removed from the batters. Ten extras arrived in the opening stand alone, and by the time Oliver was caught by Caleb Stone off Aiden Moss, Westmoor had already taken the hardest part out of the target. Callum followed soon after to Dylan Foster, and that was the first hint that the chase might not be as smooth as the opening pair had made it appear. Reece Holden and Nathan Ford tried to settle it, Nathan playing cautiously and Reece working the ball around, but Aiden Moss removed Nathan with Blake Warren taking the catch, and Dylan Foster then pulled the innings into its only true wobble. He had Reece caught by Hayden Cole, then later removed Lewis Archer cheaply, and suddenly Westmoor’s middle order had to do more than simply admire the openers’ work. Kian Brooks helped ensure that the situation never became a crisis. His eighteen from fourteen was short, but it carried exactly the right energy, a six to ease the pressure, hard running, and enough intent to prevent Ridgefield from crowding the bat after each wicket. Dylan Foster still kept fighting. His fourth wicket, Kian caught by Logan Vale, left Westmoor six down and gave Ridgefield the scoreboard respect they had been chasing since the opening stand broke. But by then the target was too small and the earlier damage too deep. Toby Lane came in with the calm of a lower-order batter who understood the equation, not trying to finish with one swing, not letting the late wickets create a false panic. He stayed unbeaten on fifteen, found two boundaries, and with Elliot Rowe’s neat little unbeaten nine, took Westmoor over the line in the twenty-sixth over. Ridgefield could point to Dylan Foster’s four-wicket spell and say they had made a contest out of the chase, and that would be fair. He was comfortably their best bowler and, with his earlier twenty-three, their most complete losing-side contributor. Aiden Moss also found two wickets, though his runs conceded meant Westmoor were never boxed in for long. Ethan Hart and Finley Rhodes leaked too many wides early, Caleb Stone had only a short spell, and once the opening stand had already removed the main danger from the chase, every later wicket needed to arrive almost immediately to change the result. That never happened. Westmoor won because they controlled the more important transitions. They did not let Ridgefield’s Caleb-Dylan stand become a full innings. They used Lewis Archer to cut out the middle at exactly the right time. Then Oliver Hayes and Callum Price made the chase small enough that Dylan Foster’s later burst could only make it untidy, not truly uncertain. Lewis Archer was the correct player of the match because his spell gave Westmoor the match’s first real advantage after Ridgefield had begun to recover. Without that control, Ridgefield could have moved from one hundred and two for three into something far more demanding. With it, they were held to one hundred and fifty-two, and even a six-wicket chase with a few late alarms still ended with Westmoor having done enough well before the finish.

At Riverside Training Ground in Lakeford, Harborford chose to field first and eventually came through by four wickets, though the match was never quite the straight low-target procession the result line might suggest, because Stonegate first gave themselves a platform, then lost the middle of the innings to a spell of pressure they never solved, and later made the chase briefly untidy through Dylan Foster before Harborford finally closed it out. Stonegate’s start had enough patience and enough small pieces of control to make the toss decision look usable for a while. Aiden Moss went early, bowled by Toby Lane before he could settle, but Blake Warren immediately brought the one burst of clean early hitting Stonegate produced, driving and cutting hard, taking the aerial option once, and making sure the innings did not crawl after the first wicket. Caleb Stone, at the other end after the early loss, looked like the batter with the clearest long-game method. He was less rushed than Blake, more selective, and much better at understanding when the innings needed calm rather than another shot forced through a narrow gap. Toby Lane removed Blake before the power of that counterpunch became a full platform, but the next phase through Caleb and Dylan Foster was the one Stonegate really needed. Dylan’s batting was slow, almost deliberately so, yet it served a purpose because it allowed Caleb to keep the active scoring role without being dragged into panic. The pair added the only stand of serious weight in the innings, and for a decent stretch Stonegate looked as though they might grind their way toward something genuinely awkward. Caleb’s forty-nine was the central batting hand, four boundaries and two clean lifts over the rope, and the slight frustration in the innings came from the fact that he fell just before he could turn a good rescue into the sort of score that changes a low-match equation completely. Kian Brooks broke that stand with Mason Cole holding the catch, and from there Harborford began to take the match back in a more systematic way. Dylan Foster had occupied the crease for a long time, but Lewis Archer would not let that occupation become acceleration. He bowled Dylan, then later took Ethan Hart and Gavin Reed, and that spell did the real structural work of the first innings because it stopped Stonegate from using their one platform to move into a proper finish. Ethan Hart made ten and looked briefly like he might hold one end. Finley Rhodes hung around for a few overs. Gavin Reed tried to survive. None of those stays became a partnership with authority, because Lewis kept one end tight and Harvey Stone kept cutting into the lower order from the other side. Hayden Cole and Isaac Dale gave Stonegate one last act of resistance, not stylish, not quick, but useful because every run after the collapse helped lift the total away from something plainly inadequate. Hayden’s thirteen and Isaac’s seven were small in isolation, yet their stand dragged the score into the mid-hundreds and forced Harborford to keep working. Mason Cole then cleaned up the last pieces, Jonah Park was left unbeaten, and Stonegate were all out for one hundred and fifty-two in the forty-third over. The score had enough substance to demand a sensible chase, but it also told the story of a side that had only one real batting phase after the opening spark. Harborford’s attack shared the work well. Toby Lane made the first and second cuts, Kian Brooks removed the best batter at the right time, Harvey Stone kept the lower half from settling, and Mason Cole finished cleanly. The player-of-the-match logic, however, sat with Ethan Vale’s intervention in the transition phase. His spell did not need a large number on the page to feel decisive; it arrived when Stonegate were trying to turn recovery into control, and his pressure helped trigger the slide that left them defending far less than they might have expected when Caleb and Dylan were still together. Chasing one hundred and fifty-three, Harborford began with the kind of opening stand that usually kills a modest target early. Oliver Hayes and Callum Price did not bat in identical rhythms, and that was exactly why the partnership worked. Oliver was steadier, taking time to settle and accepting the longer route through the chase, while Callum was the sharper presence, more willing to punish width and more capable of making the fielding side feel the score moving faster than the pitch itself allowed. Stonegate did themselves no favors either. Wides arrived in the first half of the chase, and in a defence of this size every loose ball feels like pressure being handed back to the batting side. By the time the opening pair had taken Harborford beyond seventy, the hardest part of the chase seemed almost done. Then Aiden Moss removed Oliver, and Dylan Foster suddenly brought Stonegate back into the match with the ball. Callum followed soon after, caught behind, and although the target was already much smaller, the wickets changed the mood. Nathan Ford and Reece Holden tried to settle the innings back down, but Aiden struck again, and Dylan then kept finding enough movement and enough discipline to make new batters begin under stress. Reece went. Lewis Archer, after doing important work with the ball, could not stay long with the bat. Kian Brooks briefly made the chase feel safe again through a positive eighteen, including one clean hit that eased the pressure, but Dylan removed him too, and at six down Stonegate at least had the satisfaction of making Harborford work for a win that had looked almost routine earlier. The difference was that the first partnership had already taken too much out of the target. Toby Lane arrived with the right temperament for the closing job, not frantic, not overambitious, simply aware that a few clean scoring shots would be enough. Elliot Rowe joined him and played a neat little finishing hand, and the final stand took Harborford across the line in the twenty-sixth over. Dylan Foster’s four wickets made him the clear standout for Stonegate in defeat, and with his earlier slow but useful batting hand he gave his side more resistance than most. Aiden Moss also had two wickets, though the runs he conceded around them meant Harborford were never locked down for long enough. The broader story stayed with Harborford because they owned the bigger passages. They turned Stonegate’s best stand into a middle-innings collapse, kept the total to a chaseable size, built a strong opening answer, absorbed the one wobble, and then finished with enough calm to keep the margin from becoming misleadingly dramatic. Ethan Vale was the correct player of the match because his spell helped stop Stonegate at the point where their innings could still have grown teeth. Dylan Foster made the chase noisy, and Stonegate fought harder than the halfway score suggested they might, but Harborford had already taken the match’s decisive advantages before the final few runs were gathered.
